F1.Q1: Cut stone slabs — flat rectangular flagstones of varying size, laid in an irregular running bond with a recessed joint between them. Neutral grey stone; the warm tan is the lamp, not the material.
F1.Q1_WHY:
Every unit is a hard-edged rectangle with square corners and a uniform ~4px darker joint on all sides — that reads as masonry, not tile, not packed earth, not board. When I divide the lighting out (`/tmp/flat.png`), the slabs go flat neutral grey, so the tan is a multiply and the stone is uncoloured. The bond is irregular — a course at y 208–240 runs slabs of width 40, 88, 82, 60, 44 — which is quarried-and-fitted stone rather than a manufactured module.

---
F1.Q2:
South, into the corridor mouth at x 377–442, y 400 onward.

But the ground had nothing to do with it. I picked it because it is the only gap in the wall colour — an architectural read, not a floor read. The floor gave me no steer at all: the slab pattern, slab scale, joint width, and speckle density in that corridor (x 380–440, y 400–500) are identical to the room floor I'm standing on. There is no path worn into it, no traffic polish, no debris drift, no directional wear, nothing thinning or roughening toward the exit. Walk east and the floor looks the same; walk west and the floor looks the same. In a room where the floor is the majority of the pixels, the floor is telling me nothing about where to go.

---
F1.Q3:
Almost nothing. It is a clean, intact, freshly-laid stone floor with a light scatter of grit on it.

Not one slab is cracked. Not one is chipped, lifted, sunken, missing, or replaced. Every corner is a perfect right angle. Every joint is the same width along its whole length. Nothing has been patched, wedged, pinned or bridged.

The total inventory of "damage" on ~450×380 pixels of ground is: a dark spiky stain at x 350–368, y 246–266; a smaller one at x 195–215, y 265–280; two faint scratch strokes at x 240–275, y 55–70; and a scatter of 1–2px dark specks over maybe half the slabs.
F1.Q3_WHY:
Specifically the joints. In the best-lit, highest-information part of the whole image — the slabs at x 300–470, y 205–275, examined at 5× — the joint lines are dead straight, unbroken, constant width, with sharp square terminations at every intersection. That is the signature of a floor laid last week. There is also no value difference between adjacent slabs: flattened, the whole field sits at one grey. A floor in continuous heavy use since before records began would have slabs at different heights, different tones, worn-round edges, and a hollow down the middle of the traffic line. This has none of those. The fiction says nobody has ever cared for this place; the ground says somebody finished it on Tuesday.

---
F1.Q4:
Three things.

**1. A full-width horizontal joint every 64 pixels.** At y = 80, 144, 208, 272 and 336 there is a mortar line that runs the entire width of the room, edge to edge, unbroken — and no slab anywhere ever crosses it. I measured joint continuity per row: those five rows score 0.85–0.94 (fraction of width that is joint), and they are spaced at exactly 64px with zero drift. Autocorrelation on the de-lit floor confirms it: shift the texture down 64px and correlation jumps to 0.33 and at 128px to 0.35, against ~0.1 for every neighbouring offset — and it collapses to ~0.0 if I add any horizontal shift at all. Once I saw it I could not stop seeing it. The masonry bond gets interrupted by an invisible ruled line five times down the room.

**2. The speckle.** 1–2px dark dots scattered across slab faces — heavy on the slabs at x 200–260, y 85–130 and x 490–560, y 60–100; completely absent on the slabs at x 375–450, y 215–270. It doesn't behave like dirt (it doesn't pool at joints or in corners), it doesn't behave like aggregate (it's the same size everywhere), and it doesn't behave like wear (it's not concentrated where feet go). It reads as noise that was applied, and my eye keeps counting it instead of reading the room.

**3. Soft airbrushed smudges at the wrong resolution.** Around x 405–470, y 85–120 and x 500–560, y 130–165 there are broad, blurry, gradient-edged grey clouds sitting on top of hard-edged pixel art. They have no pixel structure — they're smooth at a scale where everything else is chunky. They pull attention because they look like something has gone wrong with the render rather than like a stain.

---
F1.Q5:
**Repeated.** The slab *shapes* were varied by hand — I can see somebody deliberately mixing widths so the bond looks irregular. But that hand-work is confined inside a 64px band, and the band boundary is exposed: five continuous unbroken full-width joints at exact 64px pitch, which no slab ever bridges. That is a tile edge, not a mason's decision. A mason lays a long stone across a course line; a tiling engine cannot. The variety is decoration painted onto a grid that is still visible underneath it.

---
F1.Q6:
**YES.** It is clean, consistent, correctly lit, and reads instantly as a stone floor at phone size.

**Merely competent.** Not genuinely good. It is a competent stone-floor texture that would pass in almost any dungeon crawler, and that is precisely the problem — it is *any* dungeon's floor. It carries no information: not about age, not about use, not about the four hundred years of soldiers walking it, not about which way is out. All the atmosphere in this image is coming from the lamp falloff. Take the light off it and there is nothing there.

---
F1.CULL:
A full-width unbroken joint every 64px exposes the tile grid — no slab ever crosses it.

---
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Break the 64px seam: run slabs across y = 80, 144, 208, 272, 336 so no continuous joint spans the room width — at minimum, one long stone straddling each of those lines.
- Give slabs individual value: 4–6 distinct stone tones so adjacent slabs differ by 8–15% luminance, instead of the single flat grey the whole field currently sits at.
- Damage it. Cracked slabs, chipped corners, at least one slab sunk or missing with fill beneath it, and joints that vary in width and break down where the stone has spalled.
- Wear a traffic line: a lighter, smoother, speck-free channel through the room centre and into the south corridor mouth (x 377–442), so the ground says where four hundred years of feet have gone.
- Delete the soft airbrushed smudges at x 405–470, y 85–120 and x 500–560, y 130–165, and redraw any staining at the same pixel resolution as the slabs.

F2.Q1:
**Rectangular dressed slabs laid in running bond, with recessed dark joints — but I can only name the *format*, not the *substance*.**

I can tell you it's cut rectangular blocks about one tile tall, offset course to course, set with sunken joints. I cannot tell you whether they're stone, fired brick, or rammed earth blocks. Nothing in the pixels decides it.
F2.Q1_WHY:
The bond is legible and regular. Horizontal joint lines sit at y = 15, 47, 79, 111, 143, 175, 207, 239, 271, 303, 335, 367 — exactly 32px apart, one grid cell. Joints are a uniform 4px dark recess. Blocks are mostly 32px square with occasional double-width (64px) slabs, staggered roughly half a block per course.

What's *missing* is what would name the material: there is no grain, no bedding plane, no mineral variation, no aggregate, no chip on any corner. The only intra-slab detail is scattered 2×2 dark dots that read as generic pitting. A slab at (452,120) is a flat field of one value plus dots; so is a slab at (556,272). Strip the joints and you could not say what you were standing on.

---
F2.Q2:
**South, down the corridor at x≈376–438 — and the ground contributed almost nothing to that choice.**

Two exits: the south corridor, and a west passage at x<180, y≈145–235 (unlit floor, four more holes visible in it at (77,164), (27,229), (69,243), (159,225)).

The only ground-derived reason I have is negative: the west floor sits so close in value to the surrounding blocks that I can't read it as walkable ground, while the corridor floor is legible. That's a lighting-contrast fact, not a property of the surface.

The one genuine ground signal in the whole frame is the hole at (331,159)–(344,176) — the only hole with a straight 2px black tail running south to y≈200, plus two detached 4×4 black squares below it at ~(336,188) and (348,187). It's the single mark that implies a direction. It also happens to be the most artificial-looking thing on the floor (see Q4).

Everything else is directionless. No trodden lane, no lighter path where feet have polished the slabs, no debris drifted against a wall, no accumulation at either doorway. If I remove the lighting, **the ground does not vote.**

---
F2.Q3:
**It has been punctured, repeatedly, by one thing — and it has never been walked on.**

Those are two separate statements and both are visible.
F2.Q3_WHY:
*Punctured.* I count **22 hole-blobs** on one phone screen (excluding the `Msg` button). Their bounding boxes: 22×18, 12×18, 20×22, 18×18, 12×20, 20×18, 20×22, 24×34, 20×18, 20×20, 10×18, 20×20, 20×20, 18×20, 22×18, 18×20, 20×20, 18×20, 18×18, 20×18, 14×18, 20×18. **Every single one is ~20×20 px** — 0.6 of a slab. Not one hairline. Not one whole missing slab. Not one large collapse. Twenty-two events, one calibre. Interiors are flat `#090603` with no depth, no lip, no visible edge thickness. They read as stickers, not openings.

*Never used.* Every joint runs perfectly straight at a uniform 4px. Every slab corner is square. No slab is sunk, tilted, cracked out, replaced with a mismatched one, or wedged back with timber. There is no dirt packed into any joint. Where the room meets the corridor at y≈410 — the one place all traffic funnels — the surface is pixel-for-pixel the same treatment as the middle of the room.

For a place in continuous heavy use since before records begin, and repaired for four hundred years with rope and driven pins, this floor shows **damage without history**. Something shot it. Nobody ever crossed it.

---
F2.Q4:
Three things, and the first two are measurable.

**1 — The pale hook strokes, and specifically the fact that they get *brighter as the room gets darker*.**

Same comma/hook/candy-cane shape everywhere: (373,51)–(396,78); (495,125)–(518,142); (347,147)–(368,206); (449,211)–(500,238); (309,211)–(328,238); (441,23)–(456,46); and — most conspicuously — down in the unlit corridor around (395,545)–(420,590), where a pale hook is one of the most legible things on the whole screen.

I measured decal brightness against the local floor by distance from the lamp:

| distance from lamp | decal | local floor | ratio | **delta** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0–60px | 153.1 | 121.3 | 1.27× | **+31.8** |
| 60–110px | 143.3 | 110.5 | 1.30× | **+32.8** |
| 110–160px | 112.2 | 83.4 | 1.36× | **+28.8** |
| 160–210px | 86.2 | 54.8 | 1.61× | **+31.4** |
| 210–300px | 53.0 | 26.2 | **2.06×** | **+26.8** |

The delta is constant. **The decals are added to the lit floor, not multiplied by the light.** Under the lamp they barely read at 1.27×; out in the dark they're twice the brightness of the stone they sit on. That is exactly backwards, and it's why my eye keeps getting dragged into the corners.

The same bug makes the pale halo ring every hole — full strength on all four sides, including the side facing away from the only light in the world.

**2 — The uniform hole calibre.** Once I noticed the 20×20, I couldn't stop counting them. 22 of them, evenly spread, no clustering, no clear ground.

**3 — The tail on the hole at (331,159).** A perfectly straight, 2px-wide, non-tapering black line running down to y≈200 with a hard flat end, plus two floating 4×4 black squares. It crosses the joint at y=175 without changing. It doesn't pool, wander, or thin. It reads as a stray drawn line, not a spill.

---
F2.Q5:
**Repeated.** Four independent measurements say so.

- **The floor is one hue.** Across 105,711 floor pixels (player and UI excluded), hue spans **26.2°–29.5°** — a 3° band — and saturation 0.47–0.57. Value ranges 0.24–0.86. Stone, mortar, cracks, chalk marks, hole rims: every one of them is the identical orange-brown at a different brightness. This is a greyscale detail map multiplied by a single tint. Nothing on this floor is a *different colour* from anything else on this floor.
- **22 hole blobs, one size.** Not pixel-identical (best pairwise IoU ~0.82) — so they're procedurally varied — but varied around a single idea at a single scale.
- **Three or four stroke shapes.** Template-matching the pale marks returns non-self IoU up to 0.84 across the room. Same generator, same length, same curvature, same density in a corridor as in an open room.
- **Per-slab flat random albedo.** Sampling slab medians along a course: row y=112 runs 74, 82, **108**, 88, 90, **133**, 122, 116; row y=48 runs 86, 93, 101, 95, 101, **66**, 94. That's a ±30 value swing per slab with no spatial logic — **the same magnitude as the lamp's entire falloff across four tiles.** Blur the image and the floor is a quilt of random rectangles, not a lit room.

A made surface accumulates from causes. This one is a tint over a noise field with three stamps scattered on top.

---
F2.Q6:
**YES.** The bond is correct, the joints are clean, the pixel discipline is consistent, the read at phone size is clear. Plenty of shipped roguelikes look worse.

**Merely competent.** Not good. Good would mean I could name the stone, read where people walk, and tell what made the holes. I can't do any of the three.

---
F2.CULL:
Twenty-two identical black blobs and a single 3° hue: damage stamped on, not a surface anyone used.

---
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Multiply the pale marks and hole halos by the lightmap instead of adding them — measured constant +30 at every distance, so scratches read at 2.06× the floor in the dark corners and 1.27× under the lamp.
- Break the calibre: replace two-thirds of the 22 blobs with a range — hairline joint gaps, one chipped corner, one whole slab missing to a dark void with visible edge thickness — and cluster the survivors instead of spreading them evenly.
- Break the hue lock: give the floor at least two stone tones and cool the joint shadows off the 26–29° band, so mortar, stone and damage aren't the same colour at different brightness.
- Cut per-slab random albedo from ±30 to roughly ±8 so the lamp's falloff, not the noise, owns the value structure; keep large tone shifts for deliberate patches only.
- Put history at the doorway (y≈410) and along the corridor centre: polished slabs on the traffic line, dirt packed into the joints away from it, debris drifted at the wall bases.

F3.Q1: Cut stone flagstones — rectangular slabs of a soft sandstone or dressed limestone, laid in courses with thin mortar joints.
F3.Q1_WHY:
The floor (x 185–632, y 0–400, plus the corridor at x 376–437 running south off-screen) resolves into rectangles separated by 2–3px darker lines. I measured the horizontal joints: they fall at y ≈ 50, 79, 108, 146, 169, 207, 240, 271, 296, 336, 378 — a consistent ~30px course pitch, two courses per 62px game tile. Within each course, slab widths vary (from ~25px up to ~110px, e.g. the long slab at x 190–285, y 297–330). Corners are clean right angles; a few carry a 2px stair-stepped chip bitten out of the top-left, clearest at (299–306, 205–212). That's masonry, not poured, not natural rock, not tile.

The material read stops there. It is stone because it's laid in courses — not because of anything in the stone itself. There is no grain, no bedding, no vein, no aggregate, no visible tool marks. Sandstone versus limestone versus granite is a guess I'm making from the warm hue, and the hue is the lantern's.

---
F3.Q2:
South, into the corridor at x 376–437.

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I picked it because it is the only exit — the room is walled north (y 0–20), east (x 632+) and west (x 185−), and the corridor mouth is the one gap. That is a level-design read, not a floor read.

I want to be exact about this, because it's the most useful thing I can tell you: I flattened out the lighting and looked for any directional cue in the slab work — a worn path, a polish lane, a scuff trail, a run of dished slabs, joints packed with tread-in dirt on one axis. There is none. The per-slab brightness variation is scattered at random; bright slabs and dark slabs are distributed with no gradient, no lane, no convergence on the corridor mouth. A place in *continuous heavy use since before anyone's records begin* should have a groove worn toward its only door. This floor does not know where its door is.

---
F3.Q3:
Almost nothing. It is a clean, intact, well-laid pavement with a light dusting of incident.

The full inventory of things that have happened, across roughly 14×12 game tiles of visible ground:
- One hairline fracture, x 214–242, y 53–70 — a short dark bar with a hook at the left end, stopping abruptly mid-slab.
- Three dark asterisk-shaped splats, at (357, 257), (206, 285), and (422, 415) in the corridor mouth.
- Three small dark triangular wedges: (462, 224) pointing right, (503, 247) pointing down, (585, 352) as a diagonal chevron.
- A scatter of soft, out-of-focus blurred smudges, densest at x 415–485, y 88–120, with matching ones at (313, 130), (570, 225), (215, 253).
- A speckle overlay — fields of 1px darker dots — present on maybe 30% of slabs, absent on the rest.
F3.Q3_WHY:
Two things I'm reading against the fiction, and both are absences rather than defects in what's there.

First: no repair. The orcs have held this line four hundred years with rope, driven pins, hide and salvaged timber, and none of it has touched the floor. Not one pin, not one plank over a gap, not one slab reseated crooked, not one course interrupted. Every slab is present, level, square and in its correct course. Nothing has been prised up, nothing has subsided, nothing has been patched with the wrong stone.

Second: no administration. This is a filing system for souls and its floor bears no mark of the filing. No numbering, no incised channel, no socket, no drain, no grating, no threshold plate, no wear at the corridor mouth where every soul must funnel through.

The speckle is the tell that this is decoration rather than history. Where it appears it fills a slab edge-to-edge at uniform density and stops dead at the joint — e.g. the slabs at (455–570, 205–232) and (490–560, 330–360). Real grit pools in joints, banks against edges, thins where feet pass. This sits *inside* slabs, evenly, like a texture flag toggled per-slab. It is not dirt. It is a checkbox.

---
F3.Q4:
Yes. Four things, in descending order of how much they cost.

1. **The per-slab flat tone lottery.** This is the big one and it is what the eye actually sees. Every slab is a single flat value pulled at random from a small set, and neighbouring slabs land far apart on that range. With the lighting flattened it reads as a patchwork quilt — random light/dark rectangles with no physical cause. Worst case is the long slab at **x 190–285, y 297–330**: it is dramatically darker than every neighbour at the same distance from the lamp. My eye went back to it three times reading it as a pit or a hole. It isn't. It's just a slab that lost the dice roll. When your value noise is wide enough to fake a floor opening, it's too wide.

2. **The repeated decals.** I template-matched these rather than trusting my impression. The asterisk splat at **(357, 257)** and the one at **(206, 285)** are the same sprite, pixel for pixel; a third sits at **(422, 415)**. The triangular wedge at **(462, 224)** and the one at **(503, 247)** are the same sprite rotated. The soft smear at **(313, 130)** and the one at **(570, 225)** are the same blob. Six of the roughly ten discrete marks on this floor are two-or-three copies of three sprites. Once you catch the first pair you start hunting for the rest, and hunting for stamps is not looking at a dungeon.

3. **The blurred smudges near the lamp, x 415–485, y 88–120.** These are Gaussian-soft — no pixel discipline at all — sitting on top of crisply-aliased pixel slabs, and they run *across* the joint lines at x ≈ 430 and x ≈ 448 as though the mortar weren't there. Everything else in the frame respects the pixel grid. These don't, and the mismatch snags every time.

4. **The triangles read as UI.** The wedge at **(462, 224)** is a clean right-pointing triangle on a bright slab. It is the same shape as the "RIG ▸" affordance in the bar at y 363. I clocked it as an interactive marker before I clocked it as a chip in the stone.

---
F3.Q5:
Repeated.

The slab *layout* is generated, not tiled — course pitch is fixed at ~30px but slab widths and joint positions vary continuously across the field, so there's no repeating block. Credit where due; that part is doing real work.

But everything laid on top of that layout is stamped. Three sprites accounting for most of the marks, verified by correlation. A binary speckle flag applied per-slab. A single stair-step corner chip motif recurring across the field. And the tone variation, which is the loudest element by area, is per-slab random draw — the most recognisable "procedural" signature there is, because randomness distributed evenly is the one thing real surfaces never are.

The clinching evidence is colour. I measured hue across every floor pixel: **the 25th percentile is 27.4° and the 75th is 28.7°.** Half the floor sits inside a 1.3-degree hue band. Ninety percent of it falls between 24° and 29°. Saturation is equally locked, 0.35 to 0.56 from the 5th to the 95th percentile. There is exactly one colour on this floor. Every apparent variation is that one colour multiplied by a brightness number — either the lamp's falloff or the per-slab dice roll. A made surface has more than one mineral in it. This has one, sampled at different exposures.

---
F3.Q6:
**YES.** It is clean, correctly constructed, well-lit, readable at phone size, and nothing in it is broken. It would pass unremarked in a great many shipped roguelikes.

Merely competent. Not genuinely good.

The distinction matters here, so: a good floor tells you about the place before anyone narrates it. This one tells you nothing. Strip the magenta placeholder walls and the lamp, and the ground would serve equally well as a temple, a cellar, a barracks or a road. There is no evidence on it of four hundred years, of heavy use, of an administration, of a repair crew, or of the fact that nothing here was ever arranged for anyone's benefit. It is a generic dungeon floor rendered carefully. The lantern gradient is doing all the atmospheric work, and the moment I flattened that gradient the floor had nothing left to say.

---
F3.CULL:
One hue, random per-slab tone, zero wear or repair — reads generic dungeon, not four-hundred-year contested underworld.

---
F3.FLIP LIST:
- Kill the random per-slab tone lottery. Cut the value spread to roughly a third of its current range, and never let a slab land as dark as the one at x 190–285, y 297–330 — it currently reads as a hole in the floor.
- Introduce a second and third stone in the pavement — cooler grey-green and a paler bone tone, 15–25° off the current 28° hue — placed as patches and replacement slabs, so the surface has more than one mineral in it. Right now half the floor sits in a 1.3-degree hue band.
- Wear the traffic in. Polish and dish the slabs into a lane converging on the south corridor mouth at x 376–437: joints scoured clean along the lane, grit and dark packing surviving only at the room's edges. Give the ground a direction.
- Put the orcs on the floor. Driven pins and rope lashing across at least one fractured slab, a salvaged timber plank over a subsided course, a slab reseated at the wrong height so the course steps. Ugly, functional, and it should break the course rhythm somewhere.
- Redraw the four blurred smudges at x 415–485, y 88–120 (and their copies at (313,130), (570,225), (215,253)) as hard-edged pixel art that stops at slab joints; retire the right-pointing triangle at (462, 224), which reads as a UI affordance, and give the asterisk splat at least three genuine variants since it appears three times in one screen.
